title: FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc. (2009)
shortTitle: FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc. (2009)
summary: An agency may change policy with a reasoned explanation; contradictory factual findings and serious reliance interests may require additional justification.

sections.Parties: Fox Television Stations and other broadcasters challenged FCC indecency findings. The FCC defended its treatment of isolated broadcast expletives under the federal indecency prohibition.
sections.Material Facts: After earlier staff rulings and agency dicta generally excluded fleeting expletives, the FCC announced that an isolated nonliteral expletive could be actionable. The dispute involved words broadcast during the 2002 and 2003 Billboard Music Awards. The FCC explained that literal and nonliteral uses share offensive connotations, that automatic immunity could encourage repetition one word at a time, and that delay technology made editing easier.
sections.Procedural History: The Second Circuit set aside the agency’s orders for inadequate explanation and did not decide the constitutional issues. The Supreme Court reversed on the administrative-law question and remanded. The notes separately report that in 2012 the Court set aside the orders for lack of fair notice when the broadcasts occurred; it did not decide the policy’s general First Amendment validity.
sections.Issue: Does changing an agency policy always require a heightened standard of review, and did the FCC give an adequate explanation for this change?
sections.Holding: APA review does not categorically become more demanding whenever an agency changes course. The agency must acknowledge the change, offer good reasons, and remain within its authority. The Court found that standard satisfied here while leaving constitutional issues for further proceedings.
sections.Reasoning: The majority distinguished rescission from initial inaction but rejected a demand that the agency prove its new policy objectively better than its old one. Additional detail can be necessary where new findings contradict old findings or serious reliance interests exist. The FCC acknowledged its change and offered permissible reasons; the Court would not require unobtainable empirical research before enforcement of the congressional indecency policy. Kennedy emphasized that an agency must confront contrary prior findings and evaluate reasons in light of its experience. Breyer, joined by Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg, argued that the FCC failed to explain departure from prior constitutional concerns and ignored burdens on smaller local broadcasters. He also questioned why longstanding facts about offensive words justified a change. The excerpt identifies Scalia’s Part III-E as outside the opinion of the Court; its controlling rule here rests on the majority portions reproduced.

topics.lrs-n-hard-look: Fox preserves reasoned review while rejecting an automatic heightened standard for every policy change.
topics.lrs-n-policy-change-reliance: Fox rejects an automatic heightened standard but requires acknowledgment, good reasons, and attention to conflicting findings or serious reliance.
